newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul quizzes suspected North Korean defector.
newsitem.headline: Seoul quizzes suspected North Korean defector.

text.p: A man claiming to be a North Korean sought asylum in South Korea after arriving in Seoul's international airport from China on Sunday, and media reports said he was a former political prisoner.
Kang Chul-ho contacted South Korean authorities while in transit in Seoul on a flight from Beijing to Osaka, Japan, an intelligence official said on Monday.
He was carrying fake Chinese travel papers.
Kang said he had fled to China from North Korea in October 1992, the official at the Agency for National Security Planning, who declined to be identified, told Reuters.

The Chosun Ilbo newspaper said Kang's father was publicly executed in 1979 as an ideological foe of North Korea's Stalinist government, and that Kang was forced to denounce his father at the execution.
The newspaper, which based its report on an interview with Kang in China in 1994, said he spent 3-1/2 years in a political prison camp until 1991.

Last Thursday, a North Korean woman in her 20s fled barefoot and hungry to South Korea through the heavily mined and guarded Demilitarised Zone that has bisected the Korean peninsula since the end of the 1950-53 Korean War.
South Korea is negotiating with China for safe passage to Seoul of North Korea's top ideologue, who defected to a South Korean diplomatic mission in Beijing on February 12.

However, talks that were stalled when China observed six days of mourning for the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping last month have run into further delays since Beijing is now absorbed with its annual session of parliament, which opened on Saturday and will last for two weeks.
"We didn't get any resolution from the Chinese government so far," Chang Moon-ik, a spokesman at South Korea's Beijing embassy, said of the negotiations over Hwang Jang-yop.
"I think they are very busy because the national assembly is going on," he said.
China is wary of offending old socialist comrade North Korea, but analysts said it would probably relent and allow Hwang to go to South Korea.
Near famine conditions in North Korea has prompted a string of defections in recent months.
Adding to an impression of instability, the country's defence minister and his deputy died in quick succession last month, and the prime minister was replaced.
On Monday, North Korea's official media reported the death of two alternate members of the central committee of the ruling Worker's Party, the Tokyo-based news agency Radiopress said.

Kim Jae-bong, 72, died of illness on February 14 and Li Won-kwan, 79, also died of illness on February 24, the ruling party newspaper Minju Chosun said in reports dated late February, Radiopress said.
South Korea's Yonhap news agency said Kang, 33, stepped off a Korean Air flight on Sunday and made a request for asylum to Seoul airport police in the transit lounge.
He was travelling under a fake name using forged Chinese seaman's papers and was on his way to Japan with 11 mainland Chinese and ethnic Korean Chinese seamen to work.

"Because my father was executed publicly as an ideological offender and my mother and sister committed suicide, I was disillusioned with the North Korean system," Yonhap quoted Kang as telling investigators.

South Korean authorities have become wary of revealing personal details of North Korean asylum seekers since a high-profile defector, reportedly once related through marriage to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, was shot by two gunmen in a Seoul suburb on February 15.
Seoul police have said they believed North Korean hitmen were responsible and the assassination was intended as a warning to would-be defectors.
